article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model
citation: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6
title: The Time-Based Resource Sharing model as a working-memory model for Cognitive Load Theory that accounts for time
description: The article introduces the Time-Based Resource Sharing model into Cognitive Load Theory as a working-memory model in which time matters. Unlike slot-based models where working memory is "composed of a discrete number of slots (i.e., chunks) that can be kept active", the TBRS model "enables time to be taken into account when describing working memory solicitation". The authors use it to generate testable hypotheses about how presentation pace during learning affects performance.
requirements: Learning scenarios must be describable in terms of the pace and timing of information presentation for the model to characterize working memory solicitation.
target_learners: learners studying instructional materials with time-paced information presentation
target_learning_goals: understanding how presentation pace affects working memory load during learning
examples: The authors used the model to derive hypotheses tested in two experiments on information presentation pace effects during learning.
key_sources: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6

article_title: Development of a personal competency evaluation indicator system for tuberculosis health educators: a scoping review and Delphi study.
citation: Song Xu, Jia Qingjun, Li Qingchun, Huang Yinyan, Dai Ruoqi and Cheng Qinglin. (2026). Development of a personal competency evaluation indicator system for tuberculosis health educators: a scoping review and Delphi study. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1861732
title: Competency evaluation indicator system for TB health educators (7 dimensions, 24 categories, 63 weighted indicators)
description: A hierarchical competency evaluation instrument for tuberculosis health educators developed via scoping review, two Delphi rounds, and AHP weighting. It comprises 7 dimensions, 24 categories, and 63 specific competency elements, each with a printed indicator weight (e.g., Active Listening Ability 0.025; Medical Knowledge of Tuberculosis category 0.102). The authors state it "provides a validated tool for competency assessment, targeted training design, and workforce development in TB health education."
requirements: Expert-validated weights and the printed indicator list are needed for quantitative assessment, personnel selection, job matching, and performance evaluation
constraints: All Delphi experts were from Chinese CDCs, so weighting reflects the Chinese expert perspective; cultural/contextual adaptation is recommended before use elsewhere
The 63-indicator system has not been piloted and may be cumbersome for routine use
target_learners: TB health educators in CDCs, hospitals, and community settings
target_learning_goals: Competency assessment, training needs diagnosis, and workforce development for TB health education
examples: Table 1 prints the full system with dimension weights from 0.093 (Research and Innovation Competence) to 0.235 (Communication and Health Education Skills)
key_sources: Song Xu, Jia Qingjun, Li Qingchun, Huang Yinyan, Dai Ruoqi and Cheng Qinglin. (2026). Development of a personal competency evaluation indicator system for tuberculosis health educators: a scoping review and Delphi study. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1861732

article_title: Outcomes of team based learning in teaching medical ethics: a systematic review.
citation: Alizadeh Maryam, Bahrami Shirin, Saeedi Zeinabe, Khaninezhad Loghman. (2025). Outcomes of team based learning in teaching medical ethics: a systematic review. BMC Medical Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12910-025-01329-8
title: Six-step TBL structure for ethics education
description: The review describes a recurring six-step TBL structure used across studies: pre-class preparation, individual readiness assurance test (iRAT), team readiness assurance test (tRAT), immediate feedback (tFAT), team application exercises (tAPP), and reflection. This structure was applied to ethics topics including medical ethics, bioethics, and research ethics, using frameworks such as the Four-Box Method for case analysis.
requirements: Pre-class preparation through assigned readings or ethical guidelines
Immediate feedback mechanisms (tFAT)
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
Nursing students
Pharmacy students
Residents
examples: Studies applied the structure across diverse ethics topics including medical ethics, bioethics, pharmacy ethics, and research ethics
key_sources: Alizadeh Maryam, Bahrami Shirin, Saeedi Zeinabe, Khaninezhad Loghman. (2025). Outcomes of team based learning in teaching medical ethics: a systematic review. BMC Medical Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12910-025-01329-8

article_title: Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Xie Zhi-Bo, Cheng Xin-Yu, Li Xiao-Yan, Zhang Yi-Fan. (2025). Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07175-x
title: Team-Based Learning three-phase pedagogical framework
description: Team-Based Learning is a teacher-guided small-group learning method involving students in both individual and group activities, consisting of three phases: "preparation prior to class, readiness assurance progress, and application of course concepts". In the first phase, students complete out-of-class study through reading assignments determined by teachers. In the second stage, the Individual Readiness Assurance Test (IRAT) and Group Readiness Assurance Test (GRAT) evaluate students' readiness to apply knowledge from reading assignments. Finally, application exercises require students to apply acquired knowledge to solve problems.
requirements: Students complete out-of-class reading assignments determined by teachers before class
Individual and Group Readiness Assurance Tests are conducted in class
Application exercises require students to apply knowledge to solve problems
constraints: TBL demonstrates greater cost-effectiveness when implemented with a high student-to-faculty ratio
target_learners: medical students
health professional students
examples: TBL has been adopted by many medical schools since its introduction in 1970
key_sources: Xie Zhi-Bo, Cheng Xin-Yu, Li Xiao-Yan, Zhang Yi-Fan. (2025). Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07175-x

article_title: Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students-a scoping review.
citation: Sterpu Irene, Herling Lotta, Nordquist Jonas, Rotgans Jerome, Acharya Ganesh. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04975-x
title: TBL as a three-phase structured active-learning method: preparation, readiness assurance (iRAT/tRAT), and application exercises
description: The review describes team-based learning as a structured pedagogical method that "unfolds across three distinct phases": individual pre-class study, an in-class readiness assurance phase in which students first take an individual quiz (iRAT, typically 15–25 multiple-choice questions) and then retake it in teams (tRAT) with discussion and immediate feedback, and a final application phase where teams tackle real-life exercises applying concepts to concrete medical contexts. The review uses this framework as the standard against which it judged whether the 49 included studies implemented full-concept or modified TBL.
requirements: Individual preparatory materials assigned before class
Small teams of roughly 5–7 students and immediate feedback after tRAT submission
constraints: The review found most clinical-discipline implementations omit one or more of these steps, most often peer review
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical disciplines
examples: Table 1 of the review lists the five TBL steps: pre-assignment, iRAT, tRAT, application exercise, and peer review
key_sources: Sterpu Irene, Herling Lotta, Nordquist Jonas, Rotgans Jerome, Acharya Ganesh. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04975-x

article_title: Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students-a scoping review.
citation: Sterpu Irene, Herling Lotta, Nordquist Jonas, Rotgans Jerome, Acharya Ganesh. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04975-x
title: Implement TBL in clinical disciplines as the full concept and evaluate it against interactive seminars with rigorous study designs
description: Because most included studies used modified TBL, diverse comparators, and varying methodological quality, the review concludes that "there is clearly a need for methodologically rigorous and well-planned studies in clinical disciplines in which the TBL concept is applied as a whole". It specifically recommends future comparisons with interactive seminars and highlights the importance of training faculty in designing and delivering TBL sessions, including creating meaningful application exercises that support learning.
requirements: Faculty training in TBL design and delivery, including meaningful application exercises
Implementation of the complete TBL concept rather than partial versions
constraints: Current evidence base is limited by publication bias, English-language restriction, and heterogeneous comparators, as stated by the review
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical disciplines
examples: The review's conclusion calls for studies where TBL implementation is compared with interactive seminars
key_sources: Sterpu Irene, Herling Lotta, Nordquist Jonas, Rotgans Jerome, Acharya Ganesh. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04975-x

article_title: Comparing the effects of team-based and problem-based learning strategies in medical education: a systematic review.
citation: Zhang Weilin, Wei Jinsong, Guo Weixiong, Wang Zhongwei, Chen Siyuan. (2024). Comparing the effects of team-based and problem-based learning strategies in medical education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05107-9
title: TBL and PBL as distinct collaborative problem-solving designs differing in structure, group size, and teacher role
description: The article frames TBL and PBL as two learner-centered, collaborative problem-solving methods that differ in learning-activity sequence, group size and composition, problem nature and format, teacher role, and evaluation. PBL uses "small-group tutorials, typically comprising 8–10 students guided by a tutor", while TBL is designed for larger classes with teams of five to seven members, one teacher facilitating multiple self-managed teams, mandatory pre-reading assignments, tests of prior knowledge, and inter-team discussions with structured feedback. The meta-analysis compares outcomes arising from these two designs.
requirements: Both methods require professionally relevant problems and small-group learning as shared design features
constraints: The article notes specific implementation methods (course content, duration, frequency, group size, teacher role, learning resources) varied across included studies
target_learners: medical students
residents and healthcare professionals in clinical specialties
examples: The ten included trials spanned nine specialties including neurology, oncology, ophthalmology, general surgery, and stomatology, with TBL groups of 12–115 and PBL groups of 12–85 participants
key_sources: Zhang Weilin, Wei Jinsong, Guo Weixiong, Wang Zhongwei, Chen Siyuan. (2024). Comparing the effects of team-based and problem-based learning strategies in medical education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05107-9

article_title: A meta-analysis of students' readiness assurance test performance with team-based learning.
citation: Ngoc Phan Nguyen, Cheng Chao-Ling, Lin Yen-Kuang, Wu Ming-Shun, Chu Jan-Show, Tang Kung-Pei. (2020). A meta-analysis of students’ readiness assurance test performance with team-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02139-9
title: TBL readiness assurance sequence: preparation, IRAT, GRAT consensus discussion, appeals, and instructor feedback
description: The article describes TBL as an instructional activity sequence of three main stages — preparation, readiness assurance, and application of course concepts — in which the readiness assurance test determines "whether each participant is prepared for the next application step of TBL". Its sub-steps are the IRAT (individual MCQs), the GRAT (groups answer the same MCQs through "consensus-building discussion"), an appeals step to restore credit, and whole-class instructor feedback addressing misconceptions. The article uses this sequence as the structure across which it compares IRAT and GRAT performance.
requirements: Participants must come prepared to every session, with adequate reading materials assigned prior to class
Each student is held accountable for their contribution to team performance
The same scoring system is used for IRAT and GRAT when comparing them
target_learners: healthcare professions students (medical, nursing, dental, pharmacy)
examples: The 11 included studies all administered an IRAT followed by a GRAT on the same MCQ set, with six using percentage scoring and others using ranges such as 0–10, 0–14, and 0–20 points.
key_sources: Ngoc Phan Nguyen, Cheng Chao-Ling, Lin Yen-Kuang, Wu Ming-Shun, Chu Jan-Show, Tang Kung-Pei. (2020). A meta-analysis of students’ readiness assurance test performance with team-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02139-9

article_title: Implementation of Research-Based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study
citation: Irby, B. J., Lara-Alecio, R., Tong, F., Guerrero, C., Sutton-Jones, K. L., & Abdelrahman, N. (2018). Implementation of Research-based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 22(1). https://tesl-ej.org/
title: Transitional Bilingual Observation Protocol (TBOP) for observing pedagogy and ESL strategies
description: TBOP is a web-based classroom observation protocol based on a four-dimensional pedagogical theory developed by Lara-Alecio and Parker (1994). Originally designed for transitional bilingual settings, it has been used in structured English immersion and dual language environments and was modified to include an ESL strategies component. In this study it served "as a fidelity check to capture teachers' pedagogical delivery, and to compare such delivery between treatment and control classrooms", with trained observers recording instructional events every 20 seconds.
requirements: Trained observers; this study's observers achieved an interrater reliability of ɑ = .95, recording occurrences every 20 seconds
constraints: For this paper the authors analyzed only the ESL strategies data, not all four pedagogical domains
target_learners: English language learners in sixth-grade science classrooms
target_learning_goals: Teachers' implementation of ESL instructional strategies during science instruction
examples: Observers recorded instructional events within all domains and ESL strategies every 20 seconds across 1,380 observation rounds
key_sources: Irby, B. J., Lara-Alecio, R., Tong, F., Guerrero, C., Sutton-Jones, K. L., & Abdelrahman, N. (2018). Implementation of Research-based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 22(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1178995

article_title: Interactive Digital Kitchen: The Impact on Language Learning
citation: Nor Fadzlinda Ishak and Paul Seedhouse. (2012). Interactive Digital Kitchen: The impact on Language learning. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://digitalinstitute.ncl.ac.uk/ilablearn/kitchen
title: Bring task-based language teaching into real-world settings by embedding tasks in instrumented everyday environments rather than classroom simulations
description: The study employs the task-based learning teaching approach "brought into the real world (Ellis, 2003) instead of the artificial real-world activities carried out in normal classrooms." It combines this with digital sensor technology so that a genuine everyday activity, cooking, doubles as a vocabulary learning task. Task design also took "the involvement load hypothesis (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001)" into account to ensure vocabulary learning opportunities.
requirements: A real-world task environment instrumented to give instructions and feedback
Task design that accounts for the involvement load hypothesis to ensure vocabulary learning opportunities
constraints: The technology was still undergoing technical enhancements
target_learners: intermediate level English learners
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning through authentic everyday tasks
examples: Learners in pairs cooked a traditional English recipe, with the experimental group following system instructions and the control group a printed recipe, plus a laptop for online help
key_sources: Nor Fadzlinda Ishak and Paul Seedhouse. (2012). Interactive Digital Kitchen: The impact on Language learning. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://digitalinstitute.ncl.ac.uk/ilablearn/kitchen

article_title: The Impact of Task-Based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses
citation: Abdullah Sarani & Leila Farzaneh Sahebi. (2012). The Impact of Task-based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p118
title: Task-based language teaching as a three-phase framework (pre-task, task cycle, post-task)
description: The article presents task-based language teaching as an approach using "tasks as the core unit of planning and instruction in language teaching", drawing on functional, interactional and structural models of language. Following Ellis (2003) and Willis (1996), procedures share "three principal phases: pre-task, during task, and post-task": pre-task activates schemata and topic-related vocabulary, the task cycle has learners work in pairs or groups toward a non-linguistic outcome, and the post-task phase provides form-focused work and reporting. The study operationalised this framework as its experimental treatment.
requirements: Tasks must be meaning-focused activities where the target language is used for a communication purpose to achieve an outcome
constraints: The article notes implementing TBL in an ESP context is a challenging task for language teachers, citing Cubillo
target_learners: University ESP students (BA students of Persian literature)
target_learning_goals: Technical vocabulary knowledge in English for Specific Purposes
examples: The experimental group's classes were divided into pre-task, task cycle and post-task phases, with schema activation, negotiation-of-meaning and information-gap tasks, and post-task language focus (Appendix A)
key_sources: Abdullah Sarani & Leila Farzaneh Sahebi. (2012). The Impact of Task-based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p118

article_title: The Effect of Task-Based Language Teaching on Motivation and Grammatical Achievement of EFL Junior High School Students
citation: Islam NamazianDost, Ghassem Bohloulzadeh, Abdolreza Pazhakh. (2017). The Effect of Task-Based Language Teaching on Motivation and Grammatical Achievement of EFL Junior High School Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.2p.243
title: Task-Based Language Teaching as a communicative approach centered on meaningful tasks
description: The article presents TBLT as a subcategory of communicative language teaching developed in the 1980s, in which "the first priority should be given to the accomplishment of learning tasks rather than the mastery of language forms" (citing Skehan). Learners fulfill meaningful tasks using authentic target language, and language is acquired naturally through task accomplishment. The article applies this framework by teaching grammar through task-based instruction instead of examples and drills.
requirements: Tasks that require learners to use the target language meaningfully
constraints: The article notes a disadvantage: learners' talk is not regularly articulated accurately, and they use strategies to fulfill tasks quickly
target_learners: EFL junior high school students at pre-intermediate level
examples: The experimental group received teaching and learning grammar through task-based instruction while the control group received instruction on examples and drills proposed by the teacher
key_sources: Islam NamazianDost, Ghassem Bohloulzadeh, Abdolreza Pazhakh. (2017). The Effect of Task-Based Language Teaching on Motivation and Grammatical Achievement of EFL Junior High School Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.2p.243

article_title: The Role of Oral Communicative Tasks (OCT) in Developing the Spoken Proficiency of Engineering Students
citation: S. Shantha, S. Mekala. (2017). The Role of Oral Communicative Tasks (OCT) in Developing the Spoken Proficiency of Engineering Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.2p.161
title: Task-based language teaching (TBLT) as an approach to developing speaking skills
description: The article presents TBLT as an approach in which, per Ellis, tasks provide "opportunities for students to engage in the authentic use of the target language". The task is the principal component, providing the main context and focus for learning and encouraging language use similar to that outside the classroom. The article frames TBLT as experiential learning or learning by doing, citing Prabhu's 'Procedural Approach', and highlights Nunan's five features of task-based learning, including learning through interaction in the target language and linking classroom learning with outside activities.
requirements: Tasks performed in the target language, with learning and teaching planned around a set of communicative tasks, as Cook (2008) indicates
constraints: The article notes Norris (2009) identifies large class size, lesser contact hours, non-responsive students and exam-focused learning as impediments to implementing TBLT
target_learners: ESL learners at tertiary level
target_learning_goals: second-language speaking proficiency and communicative ability
examples: The study operationalised TBLT through a graded OCT sequence over 24 classes of 50 minutes across 12 weeks
key_sources: S. Shantha, S. Mekala. (2017). The Role of Oral Communicative Tasks (OCT) in Developing the Spoken Proficiency of Engineering Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.2p.161

article_title: Efficacy of Online Social Networks on Language Teaching: A Bangladeshi Perspective
citation: Shaila Shams. (2014). Efficacy of Online Social Networks on Language Teaching: A Bangladeshi Perspective. The IAFOR Journal of Education, Volume II - Issue II - Summer 2014. https://iafor.org/journal
title: Task-Based Language Teaching and language socialization as the theoretical framework for using social networks in language teaching
description: The article grounds Facebook-mediated language teaching in two theories. Task-Based Language Teaching treats tasks "as the core unit of planning and instruction", focusing on "communication and meaning" so learners use the target language in a natural context. Language socialization is the process where "linguistic, pragmatic and other cultural knowledge" are acquired through social experience, developing cultural and communicative competence. The article argues Facebook activities instantiate both by enabling meaningful, authentic interaction outside class.
requirements: Tasks must focus on communication and meaning, with learners interacting communicatively and purposefully in the target language
constraints: The framework is argued theoretically; the article's empirical test covers one foundation course at one Bangladeshi private university
target_learners: tertiary-level foundation English students in Bangladesh
target_learning_goals: second language listening, speaking, writing and grammar
communicative and cultural competence in English
examples: Weekly Facebook tasks called 'Contests' with Help Files, spontaneous student posting in English, and instructor correction of every student's comment
key_sources: Shaila Shams. (2014). Efficacy of Online Social Networks on Language Teaching: A Bangladeshi Perspective. The IAFOR Journal of Education, Volume II - Issue II - Summer 2014. https://iafor.org/journal

article_title: Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-Based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Alireza Hamzeh. (2016). Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 9(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p16
title: Task-based vocabulary quizzes versus traditional item-format quizzes administered every three sessions
description: The study's treatment contrast was the quiz format: the experimental group took task-based vocabulary quizzes while the control group took classic-format tests. The article states "the experimental group was given the task-based quiz and the control group was assessed through classic method (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blanks, true-false and matching test items)." Three quizzes of each type were administered every three sessions, each containing 30 items, alongside 12 ninety-minute instructional sessions for both groups.
requirements: Both groups taught by the same instructor to nullify the potential effect of methodology, as the article states
constraints: Quasi-experimental design with intact classes, which the article says violates randomization criteria
target_learners: Iranian EFL institute learners aged 19-24
examples: Three task-based vocabulary quizzes for the experimental group and three traditional quizzes for the control group were administered every 3 sessions, with 30 items each
key_sources: Alireza Hamzeh. (2016). Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 9(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p16

article_title: Developing Business Writing Skills and Reducing Writing Anxiety of EFL Learners through Wikis
citation: Mohamed Ali Mohamed Kassem. (2017). Developing Business Writing Skills and Reducing Writing Anxiety of EFL Learners through Wikis. English Language Teaching, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n3p151
title: Test of Business Writing Skills (TBWS) with 4-point rubric
description: The TBWS is a researcher-devised test measuring four business writing skills — memo, report, proposal and e-mail writing — each weighted 25%. Scoring uses a 4-point rubric covering "(1) form, (2) organization, (3) content and (4) Mechanics", for a maximum of 16 points, with two independent raters guided by anchor papers. Validity was judged by a jury of ten writing experts; test-retest reliability was r = .79, with 60 minutes recommended test time.
requirements: Two experienced raters scoring independently with anchor papers and the researcher's rubric
constraints: Delimited to four business writing skills: e-mail, report, proposal and memo writing
target_learners: Second-year EFL Business Administration university students
target_learning_goals: Business writing skills in four genres
examples: Administered pre and post to both study groups; pilot test-retest on twenty excluded students yielded r = .79
key_sources: Mohamed Ali Mohamed Kassem. (2017). Developing Business Writing Skills and Reducing Writing Anxiety of EFL Learners through Wikis. English Language Teaching, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n3p151

article_title: Completing the Task Procedure or Focusing on Form: Contextualizing Grammar Instruction via Task-Based Teaching
citation: Saraç, H. S. (2018). Completing the Task Procedure or Focusing on Form: Contextualizing Grammar Instruction via Task-Based Teaching. College Quarterly, 21(1). https://collegequarterly.ca/
title: Task-based language teaching and its three-phase task procedure
description: Task-based language teaching treats in-class tasks as the center of second language learning, with meaning paramount and outcomes assessed. For design and sequence, the article describes Ellis's three principal phases: "'pre-task,' 'during task' and 'post-task.'" Pre-task options include a similar task, observing a model, non-task preparation activities, or strategic planning; the pre-task phase acts as an advance organizer. The study operationalized this as in-class tasks, out-of-class written assignments as during-task activities, and in-class sharing as post-task activities.
requirements: Tasks must keep meaning primary, connect to real-life activities, prioritize task completion, and use task outcome as the basis of assessment, as the article lists from Skehan.
constraints: The article notes TBLT's mainly inductive approach to language structure might be problematic for adult learners, who are described as better achievers learning from information about the language system.
target_learners: Tertiary-level advanced EFL students
target_learning_goals: Advanced English grammar structures used in written production
examples: The experimental group practiced conscious-raising tasks in class and completed the task cycle with out-of-class written assignments and in-class sharing exercises.
key_sources: Saraç, H. S. (2018). Completing the Task Procedure or Focusing on Form: Contextualizing Grammar Instruction via Task-Based Teaching. College Quarterly, 21(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1169343

article_title: Tracing-based drawing method enhances anatomy learning outcomes and proportional awareness: a randomized cross-over study.
citation: Wu Yun, Li Senyuan, Gao Tong, Zhou Yipeng, Zhuang Yuandong. (2026). Tracing-based drawing method enhances anatomy learning outcomes and proportional awareness: a randomized cross-over study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10024-0
title: Tracing-Based Drawing Method (TBDM): standardized 1:1 cranial templates with transparent tracing as a transitional scaffold
description: TBDM is a structured anatomy drawing approach in which "students used standardized 1:1 cranial line drawings derived from CT reconstructions together with a transparent tracing board", tracing structures while attending to proportional accuracy and spatial relationships. It is positioned as an intermediate between passive visualization and unsupported freehand drawing, intended as "a transitional scaffold before learners progress to independent freehand drawing". Because it requires little specialized equipment, the authors describe it as a low-cost complement to digital and technology-assisted resources.
requirements: Standardized 1:1 anatomical templates derived from CT reconstructions and a transparent tracing board
constraints: The article states that if used mechanically, tracing may constrain independent reconstruction, and TBDM should not replace cadaveric learning, digital visualization, independent freehand drawing, or clinical application exercises
target_learners: first-year medical students
examples: In the randomized cross-over study, Group A used TBDM at T1 for the anterior skull view and Group B at T2 for the lateral skull view, with one-week delayed redrawings at T3 and T4
key_sources: Wu Yun, Li Senyuan, Gao Tong, Zhou Yipeng, Zhuang Yuandong. (2026). Tracing-based drawing method enhances anatomy learning outcomes and proportional awareness: a randomized cross-over study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10024-0

article_title: Teaching at scale: a mixed-methods study of team-based learning analytics to enable early support in medical education.
citation: Sheader Elizabeth, Donlan Lisa, Allen Connor, Betteridge Nathan, Dixon Michael, Gouldsborough Ingrid, Grady Ruth, Kingston Margaret, Kouskoff Valerie, Parris Kerry, Pocock Tristan, Raza Maiedha, Shore Paul, Stafford Nicholas, Tournier Cathy, Webb Michelle, Smith Michael P. (2026). Teaching at scale: a mixed-methods study of team-based learning analytics to enable early support in medical education. BMC Medical Education, 26(1466). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09612-x
title: TBL's structured weekly cycle of prework, iRAT, tRAT, application exercises, and peer review serves as a scalable template that generates routine analytics data.
description: The article describes TBL as employing "a fixed and specific sequence of activities" in which students complete pre-work, then undertake an individual readiness assurance test (iRAT) under exam conditions, immediately followed by the team readiness assurance test (tRAT) with immediate feedback, application exercises, and periodic peer review. The article notes that "TBL's structured cycle of activities (prework, iRAT, tRAT, AEs, Peer-Review) serves as a template that mitigates staff variability". This structured cycle generates frequent, low-stakes performance data that can function as a programme-level analytics system.
requirements: Requires a fixed and specific sequence of activities including prework, iRAT, tRAT, application exercises, and peer review.

title: TBL functions as an embedded analytics infrastructure that transforms routine teaching activity into a continuous source of evidence for student support, curriculum governance, and quality assurance.
description: The article proposes that team-based learning, when implemented at scale, functions as more than a pedagogy: "when implemented at scale, it functions as an embedded analytics infrastructure, transforming routine teaching activity into a continuous source of evidence for student support, curriculum governance, and quality assurance for large medical programmes". Three distinct programme-level functions emerged: early-warning signals for targeted intervention, continuous indicators of curriculum alignment and content difficulty, and convergent evidence for the validity of peer evaluation as a behavioural assessment mechanism. This framework positions TBL data not only as a student assessment tool but as a source of curriculum intelligence.

Validation of behavioural assessments such as peer review

article_title: Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme.
citation: Drovandi Aaron, Sheader Elizabeth, Kingston Margaret. (2026). Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70470
title: Team-based learning (TBL) as a structured, facilitator-guided alternative to PBL using individual and team readiness assurance tests.
description: Team-based learning (TBL) is an alternative pedagogical approach sharing many similarities with PBL, including a student-centred approach with active participation and emphasis on self-directed learning, students learning in groups and centring learning around themes on a specific disease or body system. Key differences relate to having multiple smaller groups working in a room facilitated by several academics, in a more structured and facilitator-guided learning environment. Furthermore, TBL uses individual and team readiness assurance tests (IRAT and TRAT) to support students in gauging the breadth and depth of their knowledge, supported by immediate feedback and discussion.
requirements: Multiple smaller groups working in a room facilitated by several academics; individual and team readiness assurance tests with immediate feedback and discussion.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning, gauging breadth and depth of knowledge, teamworking and application of knowledge to clinical scenarios
examples: The University of Manchester MBChB became one of few globally to use an integrated TBL approach for their undergraduate medical programme, commencing for the 2023/2024 academic year.

TBL 'supports small-group collaboration within a large class, does not require increased faculty-to-student ratios, and relies on structured materials that can be reused across cohorts with modest updates.' The study found TBL noninferior to lecture on test performance while producing higher engagement and self-efficacy, making it viable for programs with constrained staffing.

citation: Hassan Ahmed Nour Eldin, Lasheen Noha N. (2026). Impact of an integrated interdisciplinary team-based learning session of medicine and health sector programs at Galala University. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09732-4
title: Team-Based Learning three-phase structure with readiness assurance and group application
description: Team-Based Learning (TBL) is a structured instructional approach emphasizing student-centered learning through small groups. The article describes a three-phase process: "Phase 1 involves individual preparation of tasks or activities; Phase 2 evaluates both individual and team comprehension of the material through readiness assurance tests, followed by feedback, and Phase 3 encompasses group work tasks." Knowledge is first assessed individually via the i-RAT and then collectively via the t-RAT, with a debriefing session and a team appeal process. In this study the structure was applied to an interdisciplinary session on bronchial asthma across five health faculties.

Immediate instructor feedback after readiness assurance tests
Small teams with instructor support during group application tasks

article_title: Does medical students' perception of team-based learning have an impact on achieving planned learning outcomes?
citation: Jabeen Kauser, Rehman Javeria, Fatima Syeda Sadia, Ahmed Imran, Ghias Kulsoom. (2026). Does medical students’ perception of team-based learning have an impact on achieving planned learning outcomes?. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09185-9
title: TBL knowledge gains are independent of student affect: design and process issues reduce satisfaction without necessarily affecting performance.
description: The article proposes that TBL's learning benefits occur irrespective of students' affective responses, with quantitative gains (end-of-session test > iRAT) coexisting with mixed satisfaction. Design and process issues — extensive pre-reading, large teams limiting participation visibility, and peer-evaluation discomfort — "plausibly decrease students' satisfaction without necessarily affecting performance", explaining the null association between perception and achievement.
requirements: Mixed-methods evaluation capturing both performance data and qualitative perception data to detect this dissociation.
constraints: Observed in a single module at a single institution with a cohort of 96 students in a South Asian context.
Overall acceptability was modest, with only about 52% wanting TBL in other modules.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
examples: Triangulation revealed discrepancies between quantitative outcomes and qualitative feedback, providing deeper insight into TBL effectiveness.

citation: Chen Jui-O; Chang Shu-Chen; Lin Chiu-Chu. (2021). The development and pilot testing of an ACP simulation-based communication-training program: Feasibility and acceptability. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254982
title: Team-based learning combined with role play, debriefing, and reflective journaling as a training cycle
description: The ACP-SCT program organizes each week as a recurring cycle: readiness assurance testing or journal sharing, role play with standardized patients, debriefing, reflection, and discussion, with weekly reflective journal homework. Participants reported that "role-playing, as one of the components, was helpful for discovering their own shortcomings in communication skills while debriefing enabled them to identify their blind spots in the communication process." The 4F framework of facts, feelings, findings, and future structured the debriefing reflection.
requirements: A facilitator providing immediate feedback, standardized patients, and small groups of about six participants
constraints: Evaluated only in a single-site pilot with hemodialysis nurses
target_learners: Practicing nurses in continuing professional education
target_learning_goals: Communication skill proficiency and confidence in difficult conversations
examples: Each participant took a 25-30 minute role-play turn; the session ended when all six participants in a group completed their exercise

article_title: Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage?
citation: Burgess A, Kalman E, Haq I, Leaver A, Roberts C, Bleasel J. (2020). Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02024-5
title: Use the small-group, task-focused characteristics of TBL as a student-centred strategy to support interprofessional learning goals
description: The article concludes that TBL's small-group and task-focused characteristics can support interprofessional learning goals at an early stage of healthcare curricula. It states: "the small group and task-focused characteristics of TBL provided a student-centred teaching strategy to support the achievement of interprofessional learning goals." The interprofessional team-teaching format also lets educators role-model collaborative teaching and facilitate clinical application of theoretical knowledge.
requirements: teams need to work together over an extended period so team dynamics develop
curricula alignment on the shared topic
interprofessional facilitator teams
constraints: the article warns that a mismatch in student cohort numbers compromised the TBL format, and integrating new members into established teams made participation harder
target_learners: health professional students in the early years of healthcare curricula
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning on shared patient cases
examples: In the pilot, students valued interacting with students from a different professional degree, problem solving together, and learning different perspectives on a patient case

article_title: The Impact of a Pedagogy Course on the Teaching Beliefs of Inexperienced Graduate Teaching Assistants.
citation: Star W. Lee. (2019). The Impact of a Pedagogy Course on the Teaching Beliefs of Inexperienced Graduate Teaching Assistants. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-07-0137
title: Teacher Beliefs Interview (TBI) five-category classification of teaching beliefs from teacher focused to student focused
description: The TBI classifies teaching beliefs into five ordered categories: "traditional (teacher focused), instructive (teacher focused), transitional, responsive (student focused), or reform based (student focused)". Traditional beliefs emphasize transferring information via lecturing; instructive beliefs focus on providing experiences directed by the teacher; transitional beliefs stress the teacher–student relationship and supportive environment; responsive beliefs emphasize collaborative peer learning; reform-based beliefs center on students driving their own learning. The study adapted TBI descriptions as a coding rubric for concept-map terms, categorizing each term by the explanation GTAs gave during map presentations.
requirements: Requires explanations from GTAs (or teachers) about terms, because coding depends on the context in which a term is used, not the term alone.
constraints: The study applied categories derived from secondary science teachers to GTA concept maps; responsive and reform-based categories were not observed in any map in this study.
target_learners: inexperienced graduate teaching assistants in the life sciences
target_learning_goals: characterizing teachers' beliefs about student learning
examples: Table 1 codes "Describe concepts" and "Univocal" as traditional, "Hands-on activity" and "drawing to learn" as instructive, and "Relatable" and "care for diversity" as transitional.
key_sources: Star W. Lee. (2019). The Impact of a Pedagogy Course on the Teaching Beliefs of Inexperienced Graduate Teaching Assistants. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-07-0137
